summary: Hatshepsut's answer to anyone who doubted a woman could be king: a strip cartoon in stone showing the god Amun fathering her.
look: Middle terrace, in the colonnade to the right (north) of the central ramp. Along the back wall the story runs in scenes: Amun with Queen Ahmose, Khnum at his potter's wheel, the pregnant queen led to the birth, the baby presented to the gods. Wherever Hatshepsut appeared, her figure has been chiselled out, so look for the gaps.
story:
How do you make a woman into a legitimate king? You show that the god Amun is her father. Hatshepsut's artists did exactly that here, in the oldest known version of a story that later kings copied.

Amun takes the form of her father, Thutmose I, and visits Queen Ahmose. The text says she woke to the god's fragrance, the scent of Punt incense filling the palace. They sit face to face, and the conception is told with complete decorum. Amun then orders the ram-headed potter god Khnum to make the child, and Khnum shapes two small figures on his wheel: the baby and her ka, her life force. The frog goddess Heket holds out the sign of life. Khnum and Heket lead the visibly pregnant queen to the birth, and the newborn is presented to Amun, whose greeting begins 'Welcome my sweet daughter, my favourite'.

Notice that the children on the wheel are drawn as boys. Kingship had a male template, and Hatshepsut used it; elsewhere she wears a king's kilt and false beard.

About 20 years after her death her figures were chiselled away, so in places Khnum and the goddesses fuss over an empty space. The idea outlived the vandalism: Amenhotep III had the same story carved for his own birth at Luxor Temple, which you will see on the 22nd.
details: Khnum, ram-headed, at his potter's wheel shaping two small figures: the child and her ka.
Heket, the frog-headed goddess, holding out the ankh, the sign of life.
Amun and Queen Ahmose seated face to face: the divine conception, told with great discretion.
The queen, visibly pregnant, led by the hand towards the birth.
Chiselled gaps: wherever Hatshepsut appeared, her figure has been cut away.
fun_fact: The birth story was such good propaganda that Amenhotep III copied it a few generations later, with himself as the baby.
narration: Here, on the right side of the middle terrace, Hatshepsut explains why a woman could be king. Her answer: because the god Amun is my father. Follow the story along the wall. Amun takes the form of the king, Thutmose the First, and visits Queen Ahmose in the palace. The text says she woke to the god's perfume, the smell of incense from Punt. They sit face to face, everything told with perfect decorum. Then Amun gives orders to Khnum, the ram-headed potter god. Look for Khnum at his wheel, shaping two small figures: the baby and her ka, her life force. Beside him the frog goddess Heket holds out the sign of life. The pregnant queen is led to the birth, and the newborn is presented to Amun, who greets her as his sweet daughter. Notice that the children are drawn as boys: kingship had a male template, and Hatshepsut used it. Now look for the gaps. About 20 years after her death, her figure was cut out wherever it appeared, so in places you see gods fussing over nothing at all. The idea outlived the vandalism: Amenhotep the Third copied the same story for himself at Luxor Temple, which you will see tomorrow. Find Khnum at his potter's wheel, and count the two little figures in front of him.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, c. 1470 BC; Ptolemaic additions 3rd-2nd century BC
summary: Side chapels with the temple's best colour, Hathor's cow licking the queen's hand, a hidden portrait of her architect, and a sanctuary cut into the rock.
look: Hathor's chapel is at the far left (south) end of the middle terrace, behind columns topped with Hathor's face; Anubis's chapel is at the far right (north) end, with 12 fluted columns and bright paint. The ramp leads up to the upper terrace: the Osiride statues, the festival court, the solar court with its altar to the right, and the Amun sanctuary cut into the cliff straight ahead.
story:
Hathor, the cow goddess who protected the western mountain, had her own chapel here, and Hatshepsut presented herself as Hathor's favourite. The entrance columns carry Hathor capitals: a woman's face with cow's ears. Inside, the goddess as a cow licks the queen's hand and suckles her. Senenmut, the queen's steward and probable architect, had small figures of himself placed behind doors in the temple, hidden whenever the doors stood open; Hatshepsut evidently allowed it.

The Anubis chapel has some of the best-preserved colour in the temple: Anubis escorting the queen, offerings piled high, a ceiling of stars. Its 12 fluted columns are sometimes called proto-Doric, because they recall Greek columns a thousand years later.

On the upper terrace the queen stands as Osiris in a row of statues 5.2 metres tall, rebuilt from fragments. Behind is the festival court with 26 columns, the solar court with a great open-air altar to Ra, and, on the main axis, the rock-cut sanctuary of Amun. Under Ptolemy VIII it became a shrine to Imhotep and Amenhotep son of Hapu, two wise men turned healing gods, and to the Greek goddess Hygieia. The sick came here hoping for a cure.
details: Hathor chapel entrance: column capitals carved as Hathor's face with cow's ears.
Inside the Hathor chapel: the cow goddess licking the queen's hand.
Door recesses in the chapels and sanctuary: small kneeling figures of Senenmut, hidden when the doors were open.
Anubis chapel: fluted columns and a starry ceiling in blue and yellow.
Upper terrace: the Osiride statues of the queen, 5.2 metres tall, arms crossed.
fun_fact: Under the Ptolemies Greek-speaking pilgrims came here to be healed by Imhotep, whom they called Asklepios: a little Epidaurus inside a pharaoh's temple.
narration: These side chapels and the upper terrace hold the temple's best colour. At the far left end of the middle terrace is the chapel of Hathor, the cow goddess of love and of this western mountain. Her columns end in her face, with a woman's features and a cow's ears. Inside, Hathor as a cow licks the queen's hand and suckles her like a calf. Behind some of the temple's doors are small figures of Senenmut, the queen's steward and probably its architect, carved where nobody would see him while the door stood open. At the opposite end is the chapel of Anubis, with fluted columns that look almost Greek, a thousand years early, and paint that still looks fresh. On the upper terrace, the queen stands as Osiris in a row of giant statues. The sanctuary of Amun is cut into the cliff, and much later, under the Ptolemies, it became a healing shrine where the sick prayed to Imhotep, whom the Greeks called Asklepios. In the Anubis chapel, look up at the starry ceiling.

period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, reign of Hatshepsut, c. 1479-1458 BC
summary: A provincial boy who became the queen's steward, guardian of her daughter, probable builder of her temple, and the subject of 3,500 years of gossip.
look: There is no single Senenmut monument here: he is all over the site. His second tomb, TT353, runs under the temple forecourt and is closed; small figures of him hide in door recesses inside the temple. Elsewhere you will meet his block statues holding the princess Neferure.
story:
Born to Ramose and Hatnofer, literate provincial people from Armant, south of Thebes, he carried a name meaning 'brother of Mut'. He became steward of Hatshepsut while she was queen, then high steward when she became king, and steward of the king's daughter Neferure: some of his block statues show the princess's head peeping out of his cloak. He oversaw the twin obelisks at Karnak and is most often credited with designing this temple.

He prepared two tombs: TT71 among the nobles, and TT353, a 97-metre passage cut under the temple forecourt, whose ceiling is the earliest known astronomical ceiling in Egypt. His sarcophagus is quartzite, a stone normally reserved for kings; it was never finished and is now in New York.

Were they lovers? A crude graffito in an unfinished tomb used as a workmen's shelter shows a man with a figure in royal regalia in an explicit act, and gossip has run ever since. Christine Meyer and others note that he appears alone with his parents on his monuments and may never have married. In the later years of the reign he drops out of the record; his burial place is unknown, and his tombs were heavily vandalised, perhaps as part of the attack on Hatshepsut's memory.
details: Under the temple forecourt: his tomb TT353, 97 metres long, with the oldest star ceiling in Egypt; closed.
Door recesses in the chapels and sanctuary: look for a small kneeling figure of Senenmut.
Some of his hidden figures survived the purge; others were hacked out.
fun_fact: His sarcophagus was carved from quartzite, a stone normally reserved for kings, which tells you how high he had climbed. It was never used.
narration: Let me introduce Senenmut, the man most often credited with designing this temple. He was born to modest, literate parents in Armant, south of Thebes, and rose to become steward to Hatshepsut, first when she was queen and then when she was king. He also looked after her only daughter, Neferure; some of his statues show the little princess's head peeping out of his cloak. He prepared two tombs, one with the oldest known star ceiling in Egypt, cut deep under this temple's forecourt. And he dared to place small figures of himself behind doors in the temple, where the gods would see him and visitors would not. Were he and the queen lovers? A rude ancient sketch in a nearby workmen's shelter suggests that people gossiped, and they have not stopped. Some Egyptologists think he never married at all. Then, in her later years, he vanishes from the record, and his burial has never been found. Look into the door recesses as you walk through the chapels: you might catch him kneeling there.

summary: The temple that gave Hatshepsut her idea: the king who reunited Egypt built terraces against this cliff five centuries before her.
look: Just to the left (south) of Hatshepsut's temple: low ruined terraces, stumps of octagonal columns, and a square platform where the central building stood. From the courtyard, a passage 150 metres long runs down into the rock to the king's burial chamber. Usually you view it from the edge.
story:
Mentuhotep II was a Theban king who fought his way to rule all Egypt, ending the division of the First Intermediate Period; around his 39th year he took the name 'He who unifies the two lands'. The Turin King List gives him 51 years. His temple, Akh-sut, 'transfigured are the places of Nebhepetre', was new in Egypt: terraces, a covered walkway of 140 octagonal columns around a central core, a pillared hall cut back towards the cliff, and a grove of 55 sycamores in the courtyard. Whether the core carried a small pyramid, as Naville thought, or a flat roof, as Dieter Arnold argued, is still debated.

Women of his household were buried in pits under the terrace, among them Kawit, Henhenet, Ashayet, Kemsit and Sadeh, and a five-year-old girl, Mayet. In 1898 Howard Carter found the Bab el-Hosan, the 'Gate of the Horseman', in the forecourt; the story goes that his horse stumbled into the hole. Below lay a black seated statue of the king. You may find it at the Grand Egyptian Museum or still at the Tahrir museum; trust the label.

Nearby, Winlock found a tomb with 60 soldiers killed in battle, wrapped in linen marked with the king's name. About five centuries later Hatshepsut borrowed the terraces next door.
details: The square platform at the centre: the core building, topped by a pyramid or a flat roof; experts still argue.
Octagonal column stumps around it: the remains of a covered walkway that once had 140 columns.
The forecourt: somewhere here Carter's horse is said to have stumbled into the Bab el-Hosan.
Compare the terraces with Hatshepsut's next door: same idea, five centuries apart.
fun_fact: Winlock's 60 soldiers were never mummified, just wrapped, and some still had arrowheads in their bodies: a battlefield frozen 4,000 years ago.
narration: To the left of Hatshepsut's temple lie the ruins that gave her the idea. Around 2050 BC, King Mentuhotep the Second, a Theban prince, fought his way to rule all of Egypt and ended a long age of division. Here he built his temple and tomb, something nobody had built before: terraces against the cliff, a covered walkway of 140 octagonal columns, a hall reaching back towards the rock, and a grove of sycamore trees in the courtyard. In the middle stood a square core. Was it topped by a small pyramid or a flat roof? Archaeologists still argue. In 1898 Howard Carter's horse, the story goes, stumbled into a hole in the forecourt. Below was a hidden chamber holding a black statue of the king, now in a Cairo museum. Not far away, archaeologists found 60 of his soldiers, killed in battle and wrapped in linen marked with his name. Five centuries later Hatshepsut borrowed his terraces and built them bigger. Look at the stumps of the octagonal columns and imagine them roofed, a shady walkway around the king's monument.

period: Third Intermediate Period, 21st-22nd Dynasty, c. 970-930 BC; found c. 1871, emptied 1881
summary: In a cliff shaft near here, priests hid Egypt's greatest pharaohs from robbers; a local family found them and kept the secret for a decade.
look: You cannot visit it. The tomb is a deep shaft in a hidden recess of the cliffs south of Hatshepsut's temple, leading to a long corridor in the rock. From the temple terraces, look south along the cliff face: it is up there, unmarked.
story:
By about 1000 BC the royal tombs had been robbed again and again. The priests of Amun, the real rulers of Thebes, gathered the royal mummies, rewrapped them, wrote labels on the linen and moved them from hiding place to hiding place. Many ended up here, in the family tomb of the high priest Pinedjem II and his wife Neskhons: 11 pharaohs among more than 50 royals, including Seqenenre Tao, Ahmose I, Amenhotep I, Thutmose I, II and III, Ramesses I, Seti I, Ramesses II, III and IX, and queens such as Ahmose-Nefertari.

Around 1871 the Abd el-Rassul family of Qurna found the shaft; Ahmed later said he climbed down after a lost goat. For a decade they sold small pieces: canopic jars, shabtis, papyri. A Book of the Dead of Pinedjem II sold in 1876 for 400 pounds. Royal names on the market led the authorities to the family. The brothers were interrogated and tortured and denied everything, until a family quarrel in 1881 made one of them reveal the place.

On 6 July 1881 Emile Brugsch and Ahmed Kamal went down and found coffins stacked in the dark. In about 48 hours everything was out, undocumented. The steamer carried the kings to Cairo, and the story goes that villagers lined the banks wailing as for a royal funeral. Shadi Abdel Salam's 1969 film The Night of Counting the Years tells the tale. The mummies moved to NMEC in the 2021 Golden Parade.
details: From the temple terraces, scan the cliffs to the south: the cache lies in a hidden recess there.
Think of the tombs you saw this morning: Seti I, Ramesses III and Ramesses IX all spent some 2,800 years in this one shaft.
At the Luxor Museum on the 22nd: Ramesses I, stolen from this cache and sent to Niagara Falls.
fun_fact: The priests' labels on the linen are a removals log: Ramesses II was moved to his father Seti I's tomb before both ended up here together.
narration: Somewhere in the cliffs south of Hatshepsut's temple is a shaft that once held the greatest pharaohs of Egypt. By about 1000 BC the royal tombs had been robbed again and again. So the priests of Amun collected the royal mummies, rewrapped them, wrote labels on the linen and hid them, moving them from place to place. Many ended up here, in the family tomb of a high priest: Ahmose, who drove out the Hyksos, Thutmose the Third, Seti the First, Ramesses the Second and Ramesses the Third, among more than 50 royals. Around 1871, the Abd el-Rassul family of Qurna found the shaft. Ahmed later said he climbed down after a lost goat. For ten years the family quietly sold small treasures: papyri, funerary figures, canopic jars. Royal names on the antiquities market gave them away. The brothers were arrested and harshly questioned, but kept silent until a family quarrel in 1881, when one of them led the authorities here. Emile Brugsch of the museum climbed down and found coffins stacked in the dark, and in about 48 hours everything was out. As the steamer carried the kings downriver to Cairo, the story goes, villagers lined the banks wailing as if for a royal funeral. Now look along the cliffs to the south: one dark crevice there kept that secret for almost 29 centuries.
